Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette: The concrete walls of the detention cell still feel impossibly close when Amara closes her eyes. She was twenty when the men dragged her into the damp underground room, where buckets of cold water were poured over her until her clothes clung and her lungs burned. She remembered the weight of their hands pinning her shoulders to the floor, the rigid ache in her neck, and the absolute command that she obey every order without hesitation. She remembered the faces of the others in the room, the ones who did not come out with her, and the way the water had seeped under the door, pooling into a dark mirror that reflected nothing but fear. She could not say it aloud. The words would not form, only a thick, silent pressure behind her ribs, as if the memory itself refused to be captured in sentences. It felt like a broken film, edges frayed, only fragments of light and sound catching her off guard, the rest of the timeline entirely absent. Since returning to Chicago, Amara had learned to move through the world with her eyes constantly mapping the room. Before she would sit at a café or even in her apartment, she counted the doors, noted the windows, and mentally plotted every way out. She did not allow herself to drift into sleep. The night was when the water returned, when the guards’ voices echoed in her dreams, so she stayed awake, lying rigid on her back, eyes open, listening to every creak of the building. She told herself that closing her eyes meant letting the guard down, and she could not afford that mistake. If she let herself think about what happened, she knew she would fracture, so she kept the event locked away, pushing it aside whenever it tried to surface. She did not need to analyze it; she only needed to survive it again, which meant staying alert, staying ready. Her days as a pharmacist at a bustling downtown clinic demanded a different kind of watchfulness. When a fellow technician raised his voice to correct a dispensing error, Amara’s chest tightened. She stood frozen, her shoulders instinctively arching backward, her body settling into the exact same rigid posture it had held against the floor. She could not articulate why the tone felt so dangerous, only that the sudden volume made the room tilt. When her supervisor insisted she stay past her shift to reorganize the inventory, the word must triggered a familiar paralysis. She would comply, but her mind would race, counting exits, tracking every movement in the pharmacy. She began to avoid the late hours, finding reasons to leave early whenever the clock neared the time her nightmares usually woke her. She also stayed away from certain colleagues, not because of any grievance, but because one man’s build and the sharp angle of his jaw mirrored the men who had held her down. Their proximity felt like a physical weight. At home, the distance grew. Her partner noticed how she flinched at raised voices, how she would quietly withdraw when he tried to discuss their plans. Amara would not explain herself. Instead, she would sit in the dark and tell herself that her suffering was the only fair exchange for the lives left behind. She deserved the quiet punishment; it was the only way to honor those who had not survived. The guilt settled into her bones, heavy and unyielding, reinforcing the belief that she had to remain perpetually guarded, perpetually ready. Three months ago, the fatigue became impossible to mask. She could no longer function through the exhaustion, the constant scanning, the way her own body betrayed her at the slightest sudden movement. She finally sat down with a clinic counselor, her hands trembling in her lap. She was not looking for a cure, only for a way to sleep through the night without counting doors, and for the chance to look her partner in the eyes without feeling like she owed him her silence. Most of all, she hoped to understand why her lungs still closed whenever water ran from a tap, and whether the woman who had survived the dark room could ever allow herself to simply breathe.
